IB Computer Science

A3.1 Database Fundamentals

Topic A3: Databases | From “Data” → Trusted Information

The Big Question

🤔 A school stores attendance in 10 spreadsheets.

What happens when a student changes their surname?

❌ Common misconception: “Spreadsheets are basically databases.”

They store data, but they don’t enforce relationships or integrity across files.

✅ Reality: a DBMS can enforce rules so your data stays consistent and linked.

That’s what turns “data” into information you can trust.

What is a database?

What makes a database different from “a folder of files”?

A database stores related data in a structured way.

It supports efficient searching, updates, and multi-user access.

It aims to reduce redundancy and prevent inconsistencies.

Key idea

A database is the data.
A DBMS is the software that manages it.

In exams, you often describe how rules/constraints in the DBMS keep data valid.

Relational Databases: tables that connect

How can we store different things (students, classes, teachers) without repeating everything?

A relational database stores data in tables.

Each table contains records (rows) made of fields (columns).

STUDENT

StudentIDNameTutorGroup
1024Amir Khan9A
1025Leah Chen9B

ATTENDANCE

DateStudentIDPresent
2025-09-011024True
2025-09-011025False

🔗 Connection to A3.2: database design tools (schemas + ERDs) help you decide which tables you need and how they connect.

Keys: how tables stay connected

How can we refer to a student without copying their name into every table?

Primary key → uniquely identifies a record.

Foreign key → points to a primary key in another table.

Composite key → uses multiple fields to be unique.

In our example

STUDENT.StudentID is a primary key.

ATTENDANCE.StudentID is a foreign key.

If we stored (Date, StudentID) as a unique pair, that can form a composite key.

Referential integrity

What should happen if ATTENDANCE references a StudentID that doesn’t exist?

Referential integrity prevents “broken links” between tables.

A foreign key value must match an existing primary key (or be null if allowed).

Broken link

ATTENDANCE.StudentID = 9999

…but there is no STUDENT with StudentID 9999.

DBMS rule

The DBMS rejects the insert/update (or requires you to create the student first).

🔗 Connection to A3.3: transactions help keep integrity when multiple changes must succeed together.

Common relationship types

If one student can join many clubs, what kind of relationship is that?

1:1 — rare (e.g., Person ↔ Passport)

1:m — common (e.g., Teacher → Students)

m:m — needs a junction table (e.g., Students ↔ Clubs)

m:m becomes two 1:m

STUDENT —1:m→ MEMBERSHIP ←m:1— CLUB

MEMBERSHIP stores (StudentID, ClubID).

Why it matters

Relationship types decide where foreign keys go (and whether you need an extra table).

🧠 Quick Check

Identify the best key choice and relationship type.

Q1: A library table has: BookTitle, ISBN, AuthorName. Which is the best primary key?

Q2: Borrowers can borrow many books, and books can be borrowed many times. What relationship is Borrower ↔ Book?

A1: ISBN (it’s designed to uniquely identify a book edition).

A2: many-to-many (use a junction table like LOAN(BorrowerID, BookID, DateOut...)).

Benefits of relational databases

Why do organisations invest in databases instead of “just files”?

Integrity: constraints prevent invalid data.

Reduced duplication: data is stored once, linked by keys.

Concurrency control: many users can work safely at the same time.

Security: permissions restrict who can see/change data.

Powerful querying: SQL retrieves exactly what you need.

Did you know?

A relational database can answer questions across tables using JOIN — like “Which students were absent last week?”

Design decisions here affect performance later (normalization vs denormalization).

Limitations of relational databases

When might a relational database be a poor fit?

Rigid structure: changing a schema can be slow and risky.

Complex design: good table design requires planning.

Big-data scaling: joins + indexing can become expensive at huge scale.

Unstructured data: data with different shapes doesn’t fit tables easily.

Choosing the right tool

Relational databases excel when you need consistency and relationships.

Later (A3.4 HL), you’ll compare with NoSQL approaches.

🔗 Connection to A4: machine learning projects often start by extracting clean, consistent training data from databases.

🧠 Quick Check

Decide which storage approach fits best.

A social-media app stores posts where each post can have different fields (polls, images, links, location, reactions).

Explain why a relational database might be harder to use here, and what type of database could be more flexible.

Relational databases prefer a fixed schema; rapidly changing post formats can cause frequent schema changes.

A document database can store each post as a document with only the fields it needs.

Misconception Check

True or False? (Press Down)

A. “A foreign key must be unique.”

B. “Referential integrity prevents broken links between tables.”

C. “Many-to-many relationships usually need a junction table.”

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. A foreign key often repeats (e.g., many ATTENDANCE rows for one StudentID).

B: True. It ensures foreign keys refer to existing primary keys.

C: True. The junction table stores pairs of keys to represent the m:m relationship.

Key Takeaways

  • A database stores related data; a DBMS enforces rules and access.
  • Relational databases use tables connected by keys (primary/foreign/composite).
  • Referential integrity prevents broken links between tables.
  • Relationship types (1:1, 1:m, m:m) determine how you design tables.
  • Relational databases are great for consistency, but less ideal for highly unstructured data.
